transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-07-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Angela Ruiz (Zenith Head of ML), Samir Khan (Infra), Priya Menon (Security)

Summary (auto-ish):
- Deep dive on KV cache evictions and paging when running long-context prompts; explored root causes (memory pressure, fragmentation, OS swap, batching patterns) and mitigations (pinning prefixes, eviction policy tweaks, cache sizing, persistent KV options).
- Action items: Redwood to share docs and configs; Zenith to share logs and schedule benchmarks.

Topics: KV cache eviction, paging, long-context usage, prefix reuse, batching, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/on-prem constraints

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: ok, thanks everyone for joining, uh, we'll focus on the kv cache behavior you saw in prod last week. Maya and I will run through architecture details and then we'll look at the logs you sent.
[00:18] Dr. Ruiz: thanks, yeah we saw a lot more evictions when sequences got past ~8k tokens, some requests spiked in latency and then fell back but throughput dipped.
[00:30] Maya: right, that's a pretty common symptom. can I confirm you're using the default LRU eviction on dedicated, and you've got a mix of short and long contexts in the same pool?
[00:41] Samir: correct, default LRU, mixed workloads. also we enabled host swapping during heavy loads to avoid OOMs at one point, not ideal i know.
[00:50] Maya: yeah swap will kill your latency profiles, and it interacts poorly with large kv pages. If the GPU memory gets fragmented the runtime may evict sooner to free contiguous blocks.
[01:05] Jordan: quick architecture note — our KV cache sits in GPU memory and stores key/value tensors for past tokens; we shard by session and segment keys to support long contexts. eviction is triggered by memory threshold or allocation failure and we fallback to paging to CPU if configured.
[01:25] Dr. Ruiz: paging to CPU is enabled on our side, we thought it would be safer than failing. but the latency jump was very bad — 400–800ms extra per token in a few samples.
[01:38] Maya: paging helps availability but can blow latency. the runtime prefers GPU KV for speed; once we page to CPU there's an extra memcpy and often kernel queuing delays. also NVLink topology matters for multi-socket setups.
[01:52] Samir: we're on a 2xA100 setup with NVLink, but we've hit fragmentation across GPUs after several days of mixed load.
[02:05] Maya: fragmentation can come from variable sequence lengths and batching. we use bucketed batching usually, but if you have unpredictable long-context requests they can cause large allocations and then smaller ones that fit into holes — leads to fragmentation.
[02:20] Dr. Ruiz: what's best practice — separate pools for long-context vs short?
[02:24] Jordan: yes, dedicated pools for long-context workloads is recommended. it allows you to size KV caches larger and use different eviction policies (e.g., LFU or MRU with prefix pinning) without impacting short requests.
[02:38] Maya: also you can pin prefixes — for example, reuse conversation system prompts or long legal disclaimers so they're never evicted. that improves cache hit rate for reused prefixes.
[02:49] Samir: how do we pin a prefix? is that a config flag or runtime API?
[02:53] Maya: there are two ways — static pinning via model config (list of prefix hashes) or dynamic via the session API where you mark certain tokens as "pinned" for n bytes of GPU memory. we'll share examples.
[03:07] Dr. Ruiz: we also saw a pattern where evictions clustered at the same time as large batching windows — could batching be causing it?
[03:14] Maya: yes, batching can amplify memory pressure. if you batch many long-context requests you peak memory usage briefly. we recommend adaptive batching: limit max sequence length per batch and use priority queuing for long-context so they don't get aggregated with many short ones.
[03:30] Jordan: on quantization — smaller quant formats reduce per-token KV size. moving from fp16 to int8 quant reduces KV footprint but can affect model output slightly; worth testing for your tolerance.
[03:44] Dr. Ruiz: our quality bar is high for certain classes of prompts (clinical notes). can we selectively quantize?
[03:49] Maya: yes, you can have mixed quant profiles: keep critical models or layers higher precision and quantize other parts, or use model variants for non-critical paths.
[03:58] Samir: you mentioned eviction policy options, what are tradeoffs between LRU and LFU?
[04:03] Maya: LRU is simple and works well for recent reuse. LFU helps if you have hot prefixes reused many times. LFU needs counters and can be heavier to maintain on GPU, but for workloads with a lot of repeat prefixes (e.g., system prompts) it improves hit rate.
[04:18] Dr. Ruiz: we have repeated system prompts and some long patient histories reused across sessions, so maybe LFU + prefix pinning is good.
[04:27] Jordan: another mechanism is sticky sessions — keep a session pinned to the same worker to avoid reloading KV across workers, reduces cross-worker eviction and re-warm cost.
[04:36] Samir: that assumes session affinity is affordable for us; we have autoscaling beans that shuffle workloads.
[04:42] Maya: you can do session affinity with session buckets and still autoscale, it's a tradeoff. we'll show config options for sticky vs pooled modes.
[04:52] Dr. Ruiz: what about persistent KV across restarts? we had a node crash and warm-up time killed our SLOs.
[04:59] Maya: we have a persistent KV feature in Dedicated: it can spill to fast NVMe and prefetch into GPU on warm-up. That reduces cold-start re-warm. It requires local SSDs on nodes and some orchestration to keep the cache consistent.
[05:12] Jordan: for on-prem and VPC, persistence is often the best option if you have stable worker assignments and local NVMe.
[05:20] Priya: security question — if KV persists on NVMe, how do we encrypt it and handle keys?
[05:25] Maya: we support KMS integration and encrypted volumes; we can also attest that persisted caches are access controlled and rotated. we'll share the security whitepaper.
[05:36] Samir: back to the evictions — is there a way to see per-token kv usage or a dashboard metric?
[05:42] Maya: yes, we emit eviction_count, eviction_reason (fragments, threshold, alloc_fail), kv_gpu_bytes, kv_cpu_bytes, and per-session hits/misses. you can stream them into your monitoring stack.
[05:53] Dr. Ruiz: our logs show many alloc_fail events right before spikes. what does alloc_fail mean exactly?
[05:59] Maya: alloc_fail means the runtime attempted an allocation for incoming tokens but couldn't find a suitable contiguous block within configured thresholds; it then triggers eviction rounds or paging. alloc_fail is usually due to fragmentation or sudden big batch allocations.
[06:15] Jordan: note, GPU allocator behavior can be tuned — use pooling allocators or pre-allocated large arenas to reduce fragmentation. We'll share recommended options.
[06:26] Samir: earlier we turned on host swap to avoid OOMs but that masked the root cause, apparently. any advice?
[06:32] Maya: disable host swap for latency-sensitive paths. If you need overcommit protection, use eviction/paging thresholds and circuit breakers instead of swap. swap kills determinism.
[06:42] Dr. Ruiz: what about modifying the eviction threshold? we left defaults.
[06:47] Maya: increasing cache size and bumping threshold delay eviction but increases memory utilization. Another approach is tiered cache: keep recent tokens in GPU, older in pinned CPU with fast NVMe-backed pool so you don't evict to nowhere.
[06:59] Jordan: for tiered caching we recommend a staging CPU pool on machines with high-bandwidth PCIe paths. avoid crossing network boundaries for hot KV.
[07:08] Samir: we saw paging across the network to remote CPU nodes once local memory was exhausted — that's obviously bad.
[07:13] Maya: yep, remote paging will blow SLA. Ensure your configured CPU spill target is local. our runtime can be configured to refuse non-local spills.
[07:22] Dr. Ruiz: prefix reuse — is there an automated way to detect repeat prefixes and suggest pins?
[07:27] Maya: we have telemetry that can analyze session histories and recommend top-N prefixes to pin based on frequency and size. we'll include that report in the post-call artifacts.
[07:38] Jordan: tuning batching/bucket sizes: if you bucket by max length with tight bucket boundaries you reduce fragmentation. e.g., buckets at 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192. avoid having 9k and 512 in same bucket.
[07:54] Samir: we currently have coarse buckets which might be a problem.
[07:58] Maya: also consider adaptive batching with per-request sequence caps; for very long requests you might bypass batching and serve them on dedicated workers.
[08:08] Dr. Ruiz: any recommendations for logs we should give you? we attached the eviction log but what else?
[08:14] Maya: ideal set: runtime eviction logs, per-session hit/miss history, GPU memory maps (nvidia-smi -q), dmesg for OOM/kernels, and if possible heap fragmentation metrics from the allocator.
[08:26] Samir: we'll collect nvidia-smi snapshots and allocator traces. we can also run a controlled workload if you want.
[08:33] Jordan: yes please — run the controlled bench where you replay a day's worth of mixed traffic into a dedicated pool, we'll help analyze.
[08:41] Dr. Ruiz: about quantization again: we have a subset of generation tasks that are low-risk, can we route them to quantized model variants?
[08:49] Maya: absolutely — smart routing lets you send lower criticality traffic to quantized variants or even smaller models, reducing KV demands.
[08:58] Samir: curious about tooling — are there dashboards for per-model kv pressure?
[09:03] Maya: Console has per-model and per-route dashboards showing kv_gpu_bytes, eviction rates, hit ratios, and suggested tuning. we'll grant you access to a demo org for 48 hours.
[09:13] Dr. Ruiz: network patterns for VPC/on-prem — anything special to watch?
[09:18] Maya: ensure low-latency intra-node networking, avoid cross-rack memory spills, and on VPC ensure you have high bandwidth between worker instances if you're using remote spill — but again we prefer local spill.
[09:30] Priya: for on-prem deployment we need HSM/KMS integration and audited wipe of NVMe after decommission. can Redwood support that?
[09:37] Jordan: yes, we support KMS integrations, HSM via partner integrations, and post-decommission secure wipe options. we'll include checklist.
[09:47] Samir: are there kernel/driver versions that are recommended? we had one box with an older driver that behaved oddly.
[09:53] Maya: keep CUDA and driver versions on supported matrix; older drivers can have different allocation semantics. we'll include the recommended stack (CUDA, driver, docker runtime).
[10:03] Dr. Ruiz: any quick mitigation we can flip today?
[10:06] Maya: short-term: 1) separate pool for long-context, 2) raise eviction threshold slightly, 3) disable host swap on inference nodes, 4) enable prefix pinning for top-10 system prompts. those should reduce immediate evictions.
[10:20] Samir: we can do 1 and 3 today and try prefix pinning if you send the API examples.
[10:26] Jordan: we'll send a patch with config snippets and example API calls. also we'll propose a pilot config after we see your logs.
[10:34] Dr. Ruiz: great — about the bench, do you need real customer data or can we synthesize?
[10:39] Maya: synthesized workloads are fine for memory patterns; for sensitive text you can redact or synthesize. the important is sequence length distribution and prefix reuse patterns.
[10:48] Priya: for the pilot we also need SOC2/ISO docs and proof of encryption for persisted caches.
[10:53] Jordan: we'll attach SOC2 cert excerpt and the encryption whitepaper in the follow-up.
[10:58] Dr. Ruiz: ok let's recap actions.
[11:02] Jordan: recap: Redwood share KV guide, prefix recommendation report, security docs; Zenith share logs + schedule bench; set calendar for bench next week.
[11:12] Dr. Ruiz: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[11:16] Maya: thanks all, will follow up with docs and configs.

(Transcript ends)
